question: What is the memory of LLM-based agents, why is it needed, and how is it implemented and evaluated across existing work?
contributions: We formally define the memory module and comprehensively analyze its necessity for LLM-based agents.
We systematically summarize existing studies on designing and evaluating the memory module in LLM-based agents, providing clear taxonomies and intuitive insights.
We present typical agent applications to show the importance of the memory module in different scenarios.
We analyze the key limitations of existing memory modules and show potential solutions for inspiring future studies.

results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors

that is, memory sources, memory forms, and memory operations.

results.claim: Memory sources are inside-trial, cross-trial, and external knowledge; Table 1 marks which of 25 systems use each.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
the memory contents may come from different sources. Based on
our formulation
in Section 3, these sources can be classified into three categories, that is, the information inside a trial,
the information across different trials, and the external knowledge.

results.claim: Two memory forms: textual (complete, recent, retrieved, external) and parametric (fine-tuning, editing).
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote: In general, there are two forms to represent the memory contents: textual form and parametric form.

results.claim: Textual memory can be structured (tuples, databases) as well as free text; graphs are not named as a memory form anywhere in the survey.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
the textual form can be both non-structured representations like raw natural languages and structured
information such as tuples, databases, and so on.

results.claim: Retrieval memory scores entries and takes top-K; embeddings are indexed at write time with auxiliary info.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
During memory reading, matching scores are calculated
for each memory entry, and the top-K entries will be used for the decision-making process of agents.

results.claim: Retrieval methods store homogeneous information and struggle with heterogeneous information.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
retrieval methods
typically store homogeneous information inside the environment, where all the information is in a
consistent form. For heterogeneous information outside the environment, it’s difficult to directly
apply the same method for memory storage.

results.claim: Full-history textual memory costs quadratic attention time, hits length limits and suffers position bias.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
the fast-growing long-context memory in practice results in high computational cost during LLM
inference, due to the quadratic growth of the time complexity of attention computation with sequence
length.

results.claim: Textual memory is cheaper to write, parametric cheaper to read.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote: In a nutshell, textual memory is more efficient in writing, while parametric memory is more efficient in reading.

results.claim: Fine-tuning memory is mostly offline: per-step backprop is unaffordable online.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
it is unaffordable for the cost of backpropagation to
fine-tune every step of the online and dynamic interactions.

results.claim: Memory evaluation is either direct (stand-alone) or indirect (end-to-end tasks).
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
(1) direct evaluation, which independently measures the capability of the memory module. (2)
indirect evaluation, which evaluates the memory module via end-to-end agent tasks.

results.claim: Direct objective metrics: Result Correctness (accuracy), Reference Accuracy (F1 over retrieved memories), Time and Hardware Cost.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
Usually, researchers leverage F1-score to evaluate

results.claim: No open-source benchmark exists tailored for agent memory modules.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
there are no
open-sourced benchmarks tailored for the memory modules in LLM-based agents.

results.claim: Multi-agent memory is flagged as an open direction: synchronization, communication, information asymmetry.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
One pivotal aspect that emerges in
the cooperative scenarios is memory synchronization among agents. This process is fundamental
for establishing a unified knowledge base, ensuring consistency in decision-making across different
agents.

results.claim: Lifelong learning needs temporal memory, large-scale storage and forgetting.
results.setup: Survey of LLM-agent memory papers up to early 2024; no experiments run by the authors
results.quote:
lifelong learning is temporal, necessitating that an agent’s memory captures
temporality.

limits: Survey only: no experiments, no quantitative comparison of memory designs; Tables 1-3 are check-mark taxonomies of 25 systems.
The cached PDF is arXiv v1 (Apr 2024, 'Preprint. Under review'), not the TOIS 2025 version; later content (graph-based memory, benchmarks) may exist only in the published version.
Knowledge graphs are not a category: only a passing mention of CMeKG used for fine-tuning (Sec 7.6) and tuples/databases as structured text. No treatment of graph memory shared between agents.
Authors concede no open-source benchmark for memory modules (Sec 6.3) and that indirect task evaluation confounds memory with other factors.
Multi-agent memory (Sec 8.2) is a short future-direction paragraph with no taxonomy of shared stores.
Systems covered end around early 2024; MemGPT, Generative Agents, Reflexion etc. are the newest it describes.
practices: Do not concatenate the whole history into the prompt; add a memory module (Sec 5.2.1, p15).
Use retrieval (embedding index plus top-K, combining relevance, recency, importance) to bring back distant but relevant memories (Sec 5.2.1, p15-16).
Treat memory as three operations, write, manage (merge, reflect, forget), read, and design them together since write form constrains read (Sec 5.3, p18-20).
Extract and summarise at write time because raw observations are lengthy and noisy (Sec 5.3.1, p18).
Use textual memory for recent/context-specific tasks and parametric memory for large or well-established knowledge (Sec 5.2.3, p18).
Use knowledge editing rather than fine-tuning for small online memory updates (Sec 5.2.2, p17).
Evaluate memory both directly (correctness, F1 on retrieved references, time and peak GPU memory) and indirectly via ablation with/without memory (Sec 6, p20-23).
For personal assistants prefer textual retrieval memory (Sec 7.2, p25).

terms.definition: The complete agent-environment interaction process is called a trial, and each interaction turn is called a step.
the memory of the agent is only relevant to the historical information within the same trial.
memory information at step t comes from three sources: inside-trial history, cross-trial history, and external knowledge D.
project the raw observations into the actually stored memory contents, m = W({a, o}).
process the stored memory information to make it more effective (summarising, merging, forgetting), M_t = P(M_t-1, m_t).
obtain important information from the memory to support the next agent action, usually by similarity between M and next-action context.
information is explicitly retained and recalled by natural languages (complete, recent, retrieved, external).
the memory information is encoded into parameters and implicitly influences the agent’s actions (fine-tuning, editing).
accuracy of answers to pre-defined questions based on the memory module.
whether the agent retrieves relevant memory contents, scored by F1 against ground truth.
